additional_context:
[Council feedback on the previous definition]
From model_reviewer:
- authoring_response.proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.stabilization_demands: The frames show a straight-body plank on the toes with a wide stance. The instructions say to keep the body straight and extended and to widen the feet for support. No hip, pelvic or leg demand is present, so glutes, hip flexors, quadriceps, hamstrings and calf/ankle muscles are all explicit zeros. The legs and hips hold the body line against gravity and resist rotation during each row, so this is a materially wrong muscle pattern. Suggested correction: Add demands that reach the lower body. Options are pelvic_alignment, anti_extension_hip and, for the plank-holding legs, knee_joint_stability, ankle_stability or femoral_head_stabilization, plus intra_abdominal_pressure if bracing is intended. Choose whichever fits the evidence. Consider an isometric knee-extension or hip-extension hold only if it can be justified.
- authoring_response.proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.stabilization_demands: The assumptions say the support-side push into the floor is treated as stabilization, but no demand covers it. The supporting arm holds a locked-out, loaded plank position. The frames show the elbow extended and the shoulder under compression. The tracer gives the triceps lateral and medial heads, clavicular deltoid and clavicular pectoralis major no involvement, and the long head of triceps and sternocostal pectoralis only incidental synergist credit from glenohumeral extension. Suggested correction: Add support-arm demands such as shoulder_position_hold and elbow_joint_integrity or elbow_stability, so the pressing/bracing role of the supporting side is represented. Keep wrist_stability and grip. Consider whether an isometric elbow extension action with assist emphasis is warranted.
[End of council feedback]

assumptions: Laterality is bilateral because the arms alternate across the set, so each arm rows and each arm supports. Actions are therefore marked as working and one_sided_limbs is empty.
Joint actions describe the exertion phase of the rowing arm: elbow flexion, shoulder extension and scapular retraction, as the instructions say to retract the shoulder blade while flexing the elbow.
The supporting arm pushes into the floor with the elbow locked out. This is modeled as an assist-level elbow extension hold plus shoulder_position_hold and scapular_anchoring.
Kinetic chain is open_chain because the rowing hand moves the kettlebell freely off the floor. The body stays supported by the feet and the other hand, so this is a judgment call.

The legs and trunk hold a rigid plank, so no hip or lumbar motion is listed. The lower body works through pelvic_alignment, anti_extension_hip, femoral_head_stabilization, knee_joint_stability and ankle_stability because of the wide toe stance.
The trunk resists rotation and extension during each row, so anti_rotation_torso, anti_extension_spine and intra_abdominal_pressure are included.
Grip and wrist_stability are included because the loads are held in the hands.
classification_reasons: The frames show a wide-stance toe plank with both hands on kettlebell handles. One kettlebell is rowed to the hip while the other hand stays on the floor, matching the instructions.
Every joint action and stabilization demand needed is available in the schema vocabulary.

instructions: Place two kettlebells on the floor about shoulder width apart. Position yourself on your toes and your hands as though you were doing a pushup, with the body straight and extended. Use the handles of the kettlebells to support your upper body. You may need to position your feet wide for support.
Push one kettlebell into the floor and row the other kettlebell, retracting the shoulder blade of the working side as you flex the elbow, pulling it to your side.
Then lower the kettlebell to the floor and begin the kettlebell in the opposite hand. Repeat for several reps.
source.name: Alternating Renegade Row
